title: Mojo: MLIR-based Performance-Portable HPC Science Kernels on GPUs for the Python Ecosystem
problem: Scientific Python ecosystem lacks portable GPU programming with C-like performance. CUDA/HIP require language switching and target single vendors. Python abstractions (CuPy, Numba) sacrifice performance. Need for high-performance, portable, Python-integrated GPU programming.
motivation: Scientists prefer Python for productivity but need GPU performance portability across NVIDIA and AMD architectures without sacrificing computational efficiency.
method: Mojo is a programming language that compiles Python-like code to run on GPUs using MLIR, an intermediate compiler format that translates the same code to work on different GPU types without rewriting. It uses syntax similar to CUDA (the standard GPU programming language) so experienced GPU programmers can learn it quickly. The researchers tested this on four scientific computing tasks: stencil and BabelStream (where moving data between memory and processors is the limiting factor) and miniBUDE and Hartree-Fock (where actual computation is the bottleneck, with Hartree-Fock also using atomic operations to safely coordinate multiple processors updating shared data).
key_novelty: Mojo shows that MLIR-based compilation can give the Python scientific ecosystem portable, high-performance GPU code that works across different vendors.
contributions: Mojo MLIR-based GPU programming for scientific workloads
Evaluation on NVIDIA H100 and AMD MI300A GPUs
Competitive performance with CUDA on memory-bound kernels
Identified performance gaps on AMD GPUs for atomic operations
Gaps on both platforms for compute-bound kernels with fast-math
limitations: Limited evaluation set (4 kernels); gaps on atomic operations and fast-math suggest incomplete optimization; learning curve remains fairly low-level; AMD MI300A gaps may indicate immaturity.
